hypothesis: The four prior stability failures share a common pattern: gait_phase_regularity_reward_weight (−1.0, contributing −1.479 per step) is a large competing penalty that overrides the policy's ability to take stabilising recovery steps, without actually improving CV metrics (which have worsened across all runs). Simultaneously, limb_symmetry_velocity_weight=0.1 makes the velocity-asymmetry component of the symmetry reward negligibly small (~−0.006 per step), so the mirror-pose limp (symmetry_pos_cost~0.003, symmetry_vel_cost~0.098) has been unaddressed. Reducing gait_phase_regularity to −0.3 relieves the competitive pressure on balance, while increasing limb_symmetry_velocity_weight to 0.6 activates a meaningful signal against the velocity desynchronisation that is driving irregular contact timing and high gait CV.
expected_effects: fell_over_rate drops below 0.5 past iteration 750 — primary pass criterion; removing the large gait_phase_regularity competing penalty frees the policy to take recovery steps
symmetry_vel_cost_mean decreases from ~0.098 baseline — directly targeted by the velocity_weight increase; if it does not decrease, the limb_symmetry weight change is not taking effect
gait_contact_cv_mean decreases from ~0.568 toward <0.4 — more synchronised leg velocity phases should produce more regular stance timing
gait_phase_regularity reward contribution becomes less negative (smaller magnitude than the current −1.479) — confirming the weight reduction is reflected in the reward signal

track_linear_velocity reward holds stable or improves slightly — with less competing penalty pressure, the policy can allocate more capacity to tracking; any decrease here would be unexpected and worth investigating
